passage: Note, Sunday night. After Vaibhav's bad chemistry result on Friday, I watched him write a new timetable and pin it above the desk: lights out at nine at night, up at four in the morning, from the very next day. No half-measures. On Monday the alarm rang at four and he was up, grey-faced, and fell asleep on the sofa by five in the afternoon. On Tuesday the alarm rang and he did not get up. He dropped the timetable in the bin and said, "I can't even do this." What I did: I took it out of the bin, told him the plan was too big for anyone and not a sign of weakness, and asked if we could pick one small change together. He shrugged but sat down with me. We chose one thing: the same wake time every day. - Hansa

Friday, 11:50 pm

Day two of the New Me plan, and it's already dead.

After the maths paper on Wednesday I came home furious with myself. I wrote a timetable in red pen: sleep at 9 pm, wake at 4 am, study two hours before school. Starting the very next day. Dolma said, "Mehak, you sleep at one. That's a huge jump." I told her she didn't get it.

Thursday I lay in bed at nine staring at the fan till past midnight. Alarm at four. Hit snooze till six. Slept through chemistry.

Tonight I didn't even try. I'm writing this at midnight and I feel like the biggest failure. Two days. I couldn't even do two days.

Maybe Dolma was right. Maybe the plan was the failure, not me. I don't know. I'm too tired to know.

How is Mehak feeling as the entry is written?
qa.a: Mehak feels like a failure, tired and discouraged, though starting to wonder whether the plan itself was the problem.

qa.q: What would be a better approach than a sudden 9 pm bedtime?
qa.a: Keeping a fixed wake time and moving bedtime earlier in small steps, so the body clock has time to adjust.

qa.a: Dolma probably saw it coming and feels sympathetic rather than smug, since the warning was about the huge jump, not about Mehak.
